prompt: Write a cranky blog post about trying a bunch of new web calendar apps and finding that none of them do what you need. Include a theory about why so many of them exist.
Write a personal essay about the meaning of life, framed around a workshop or dinner conversation. I'm tired of tidy answers and want something thoughtful.

I'm a psychiatrist and patients keep asking me to certify their pets as emotional support animals. Write a candid, funny essay from the clinician's side about how that system really works and what's wrong with it, even if the outcome is mostly harmless.

I just found out some online forum members pool money to synthesize experimental drugs and try them on themselves. It's obviously reckless, yet I feel weirdly pleased it exists. Write a short blog post making sense of that mixed reaction.

People on Twitter are sharing their salaries publicly this week. You've had an unusual tech career: a Japanese salaryman job, a consulting practice, a few small software businesses. Write a candid post that makes the case for talking openly about pay and puts your own numbers on the table, with whatever lessons you think younger engineers should take from them.

Everyone says reusing other people's code is good and reinventing the wheel is bad. Is that actually true? Write a blog post on when a software company should build things itself versus buy or outsource.

Write something atmospheric and a bit unhinged: a person who normally avoids San Francisco ends up walking its streets alone in the dark just before sunrise, and the city starts to feel like the place where the world ends. Feel free to bring in poetry.
Tell the origin story of how a musician selling his own CD online accidentally started a business. Write it as a blog post.

Write an essay about what it means for a category or definition to be wrong. Can you ever say a word like 'fish' or 'planet' is used incorrectly, or is it all convention? Use whatever examples you like, and carry the argument through to a place where it actually matters in real life.

Use a thought experiment about a town founded by people who hate late-night noise to think through when a community has the right to restrict what its members do, and then apply it to the housing and NIMBY debate. Write it as a long, exploratory blog post with a libertarian-ish flavor, ending with a practical proposal.

Software teams keep arguing about who should write the spec and who should own product design. Write an essay about where that job should sit in an organization, who to hire for it, and who not to, drawing on any big-company experience you have.

Tyler Cowen argued that because nobody can predict what AI will do, we should stop worrying about existential risk and just take the plunge. Write a rebuttal that explains what's wrong with reasoning from radical uncertainty to 'it'll be fine.'

It's late 2005 and everyone in tech is throwing around the phrase "Web 2.0." You've been skeptical of it, and you run a firm that funds early-stage web startups. Write an essay working out whether the term actually means anything, and if so, what.

You've started selling programming zines on the side, and most of your sales come from posting comics on Twitter. Write a candid, early-stage blog post working through marketing: what it's actually for, which common internet marketing tactics you'd use or avoid, and how to tell people about your work without being annoying.

I saw a claim that bisexual people report long COVID far more often than heterosexuals. Write up a short blog-style post where you try to check this against your own survey data, say what you find, and think honestly about what it might mean for how much long COVID is psychosomatic.

Everyone is excited about psychedelics as a treatment for depression and trauma right now. Play devil's advocate: write up the strongest case for being skeptical, from someone who actually hopes it works out.

There's a study where telling elderly people they carry an Alzheimer's risk gene made their memory scores worse. Write a blog post that looks at whether the conclusion, that genetic testing itself can harm people, actually follows.

I've only ever heard that American health care is bad and everyone else's is fine. I'm about to read a big comparative book on national health systems. Write a review in your own voice: what the different systems actually look like, what's surprising about how they compare, and whether the book really teaches you anything.

I keep noticing that more and more things in my life feel 'addictive' -- the internet, games, food. Is the world actually getting more addictive, and if so what should a person do about it? Write me an essay.

Is there a biological explanation for why people with anorexia can't just regain weight once they decide to? Speculate about it using what we know about obesity and the body's weight set point. Flag clearly that you're not an expert.

Lately everything is a kind of 'justice': economic justice, climate justice, intergenerational justice. Write a short essay on what changes, psychologically and morally, when we reframe helping people as pursuing justice.
Newspapers, record labels and book publishers all complain that people won't pay for content anymore. Write an essay on whether that framing is even right, and what happens to publishing next.

Libertarians like to say that competition between private communities, each trying to offer the best rules, will protect freedom better than government can. The internet looks like a real-world test of that idea. Write an essay on whether it actually has, especially for unpopular speech.

Write a post for software developers who have never thought about operations: what is it, how does your understanding of it tend to evolve, and how can an ordinary developer start getting better at it?

Do car makers actually build safe cars, or do they just build cars that score well on the crash tests everyone knows about? One way to find out is to look at what happened when the IIHS introduced new tests, like the driver-side small overlap test in 2012 and the passenger-side version in 2018. Write up an analysis along those lines: which manufacturers held up, what that suggests, and what caveats someone should keep in mind before reading too much into crash test scores.

Why do people believe in conspiracy theories? I'm not satisfied with 'they're stupid and hateful.' Write an essay that tries to break the phenomenon into smaller cognitive and emotional parts, the way you'd ask what kind of mistakes would make an AI believe them.
Rat Park is usually cited as proof that addiction is caused by misery and deprivation. Write a skeptical essay examining whether that story holds up.
Give a talk-style essay to an audience of startup founders on whether being genuinely good to users and the world is a sound business strategy, not just a nice sentiment.
Why did prehistoric people all over the world drill holes in each other's skulls, and why did so many survive? And why did the practice die out? Give me your best attempt at solving the mystery.

You've spent years preaching slow, profitable, bootstrapped growth, and now you're about to take venture capital for a new company. People are shocked. Write a post explaining how you decide whether a business should or shouldn't raise VC.

I spent three months at a programming retreat where beginners improved absurdly fast, and I'm convinced a big part of it was the culture around asking for and giving help. Write a short, punchy blog post about why help matters so much in a community or workplace, aimed at teams that treat questions as interruptions.
You just got told in a performance review that you're very good at debugging hard problems, and you didn't used to be. Write a blog post reflecting on what changed.

Write a blog post about trying to replicate a psychiatry study that claimed a certain snack food could trigger manic episodes, using data from a big reader survey. Be honest about what the data can and can't show.

Joel Spolsky famously argued that great developers are basically never on the job market, so the resume pile is mostly people nobody else wanted. Write an essay pushing on that claim. Is developer hiring really a 'market for lemons' in Akerlof's sense, and if hiring managers keep saying they can't find good people, what's actually going on?

Congressional voting data gets turned into a left-right scale without anyone telling the algorithm what left and right are. Could something like that work for morality? Write an essay exploring whether you could discover what 'good' means statistically from ordinary life decisions.
You co-founded Y Combinator and have advised hundreds of startups through it. Write a reflective essay on what you've learned from your own 'users', the founders you've funded.

I've been reading about how therapy and psychedelics supposedly change deep emotional beliefs that plain evidence can't touch. Write an essay on why the mind seems to keep some of its beliefs walled off from each other, what that says about mental illness, and whether it also explains why smart, informed people fail to change their minds.
How do you know when it's time to sell your company? Answer with your own story rather than a checklist.

Every few months a headline says some food is as bad as smoking or raises your mortality by 20%. Write a piece on how to make sense of those numbers, using the processed-meat scare as the worked example. I want to know how much it actually matters.

Write a short essay on not voting as a deliberate political act. Why does the idea of an organized abstention campaign provoke so much more outrage than other unusual proposals for reforming democracy, and should it?

You run a startup accelerator. Lately a lot of successful founders have told you that the standard advice for scaling a company, hire good people and give them room, nearly wrecked their businesses. Write an essay about why that advice might be wrong for founders and what the alternative could look like.

You've been posting simple hand-drawn comics about Linux every day, and a commenter called them childish and asked why anyone likes them when Wikipedia exists. Write a short blog post answering that honestly.

You run a program that funds startups at the very earliest stage, when they're often just the founders. People describe what you do as "seed funding," and you've started to feel that's misleading. Write an essay figuring out what a very early stage investor actually does and why it's a different kind of thing from venture capital.
The Pope just got named Time's Person of the Year. Write a short, wry blog post on how you feel about the way people react to his humble gestures.
Write a darkly funny blog post that retells the Thanksgiving story (Squanto, the Pilgrims, the plague) as though it belonged to a different genre than the one it's taught in.
Write a blog post criticizing a common design flaw in psychology experiments, using the debate over violent video games as the starting point. I want it to be skeptical but fair to the researchers.
Everyone treats being on call as pure misery. Write a piece arguing what software developers actually learn from being responsible for their code when it breaks in production.

I've seen 'devops' on job postings for years and honestly have no idea what it's supposed to mean beyond 'uses Chef and Puppet'. Write a blog post figuring out what devops actually is and why someone might find it exciting.

Write a personal essay, in the first person, about why someone who has experienced harassment at work might stay silent about it for years, and why the usual media coverage of these stories can make that silence worse rather than better.

Write a blog post encouraging engineers to tell a colleague's manager when that colleague does great work, especially as a way to support people from underrepresented groups. Cover when it matters, how to do it well, and what can go wrong.
There's a stereotype that the left thinks problems are social and fixable while the right thinks they're biological and fixed. Write an essay arguing about whether that gets things backwards.

I've just finished Infinite Jest and I'm still puzzled. Write a long, funny, opinionated review for people who've read it (spoilers fine) that tries to say what the book is actually about and how its structure relates to that.
Suppose a city wanted to become the next Silicon Valley. Is that even possible, and if so what would it really take? Write an essay working out what actually causes a technology hub to form.

Last week I wrote about funding structures that line up innovation with business, and the most common reply was 'isn't that what B Corps are for?' Write a follow-up post on why 'doing good' shouldn't be defined by tax status or labels.

Why do street drugs like ketamine and MDMA keep turning out to be better psychiatric treatments than what pharmaceutical companies produce on purpose? I want a speculative blog post that tries a few explanations and says honestly where they might fail.

Write an essay arguing that procrastination isn't always a vice. I'm interested in the distinction between the kinds of things people put off and what they do instead, and what that means for someone who wants to do ambitious work.

If you could only give startup founders a dozen or so pieces of advice, one sentence each, what would they be? Write it up with a short explanation under each, and tell me which one you'd keep if you could only keep one.

A popular article argued that military intervention is a wasteful way to help foreigners because the same money donated to a top charity would save more lives. I think the argument is flawed. Write a rebuttal that actually does the cost-effectiveness arithmetic.

A lot of people tell me they'd like to start a technical blog but don't know what to write about that anyone would find useful. Write an essay on one good answer to that: using the things you've personally struggled with as the source of posts.

I finally got around to reading The Black Swan, years after everyone else. Write me a book review that engages with the ideas rather than summarizing them, including where you think Taleb is right and where his advice might be dangerous. Some humor welcome, since reviewing him seems like a risky business.

A friend of mine is a talented artist who feels stuck and keeps doing what he thinks he's supposed to do, even though it clearly isn't working. I suspect he's making his life harder than it needs to be through how he frames his options. Write an essay about how our unexamined assumptions about what a good life or career must look like limit us, and what to do about it.

You've been running a small software business that sells to teachers for a few years, mostly in spare hours around a brutal Japanese salaryman job, and you're about to quit to go full time. Write a long, practical blog post for programmers who want to run a business on the side with only a few hours a week: what actually lets you pull it off?

I'm in the second year of a PhD and keep hearing that what separates good researchers is 'research taste', the ability to pick good problems. Nobody tells you how to actually get better at it. Can you write something practical on how to deliberately develop research taste, including the common ways people go wrong?

An economist I read argues that psychiatric illnesses like alcoholism, ADHD and schizophrenia are best understood as unusual preferences rather than diseases, since they don't look like the 'budget constraints' that physical illnesses are. You're a practicing psychiatrist. Write a thorough reply explaining where that argument goes wrong.

Someone wrote to a famous songwriter saying she didn't know who she was and so couldn't make art. He told her she didn't need to know. Write an essay on whether self-knowledge matters for creative work, and how people actually come to know themselves.

Everyone in crypto is proposing new governance models, but they nearly all boil down to some form of voting. Write a post questioning that: what's wrong with voting as a governance mechanism, especially for decentralized communities, and what could replace it?

It's the day before the 2016 US election and the race looks close. I'm worried everyone will draw sweeping conclusions about the country from whichever way it falls. Write a short essay on how we should think about what the result will mean.

Americans spend more on almonds than on all of election campaigns, which has always puzzled me. Write a post that explains how political money really works, who has figured out how to use it, and what that means for AI regulation.
